shape RunningActivityShape:
    description:
        What counts as work still running in the application, and how each is
        listed, newest last.

    running:
        - the task the harness is working on, from the @{PromptEditor}, headed "Task" with the first line of its prompt
        - each question still running, from the @{ChatInputScope}'s Ask tab, headed "Question" with its first line
        - a spec build run on its own, as the @{SpecBuildScope} says, "Building the spec"
        - a divergence analysis in the @{DivergenceScope}, "Analyzing divergence"
        - a search for concepts to rescope in the @{RescopeScope}, "Finding scopes to extract"

        Prompts waiting in the queue don't count as running, since they are
        saved with the project, and neither does a panel whose work is over.

        Tasks, questions, and spec builds count in every open project of the
        @{OpenProjectsScope}, not only the one on screen. Those of the project
        on screen come first, then each other project's, its rows headed with
        that project's folder name after the kind, such as
        "Task · my-project".

    indicator:
        While anything is running, a small spinner shows, with how many things
        are running beside it when more than one is. Its tooltip says what is
        running, or how many things are. While nothing is, neither shows, and
        nothing takes their place. Where it sits is up to what holds it.

    list:
        Clicking the spinner opens a small list beneath it of everything
        running, one row each, in the order above, each with a small spinner of
        its own. Clicking a row closes the list and reveals what it is, first switching to
        its project when it belongs to another:
        - a task brings back the latest task's output, closing the previous tasks and any inset panel over it, and scrolls it to the end

export ui-component RunTargetsScope:
    concept: {RunTargetsConcept}

concept RunTargetsConcept:
    pitch:
        Makes the project runnable from the application, whatever kind of
        project it is: the harness finds out once how the project is built,
        run, and tested, that understanding is saved with the project, and
        each way of running it becomes a button in the ribbon's Code tab.

    shape: {RunTargetsShape}

shape RunTargetsShape:
    description:
        A project's run targets are the ways it can be run, each a name and a
        shell command, run in the project directory: for a Rust project,
        "Run" as `cargo run`, "Build" as `cargo build`, and "Test" as
        `cargo test`; for a C++ project built with CMake, "Run" as configuring
        and building with `cmake`, then running the binary it built; and so
        on for whatever the project is.

    kinds:
        Each target is of a kind, which picks its icon:
        - run, which runs the project, with a play icon
        - build, which only builds it, with a hammer icon
        - test, which runs its tests, with a flask icon
        - other, anything else, with a terminal icon

    finding:
        overview:
            Nothing about a project's targets is guessed by the application
            itself. Finding them is agentic: a @{OneOffAgentRunScope}, whose
            prompt is run-targets.pi, of the @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, looks
            through the project, its build files, manifests, and readme, and
            replies with its targets, the way to run the project first. Its
            command runs the project from scratch, building first when it has
            to, so it works on a fresh clone.

        saving:
            Once found, the targets are saved with the project's data, as the
            @{ProjectDataScope} says, in run.json, and read from there from then
            on, every time the project is opened: they aren't found again
            unless asked. run.json is kept with the project, so everyone
            working on it has the same buttons, and can be edited by hand; one
            that can't be read counts as no targets found.

        reply:
            The harness replies with JSON listing each target's name, command,
            and kind. A target with no name or no command is left out, as is a
            kind that isn't one of the four, which counts as other. A reply
            with no targets at all fails, saving nothing.

    panel:
        overview:
            Finding and running are shown in one @{MinimizablePanelScope},
            titled "Run", which holds one thing at a time: finding the targets,
            or running one of them.

        whileFinding:
            While finding, the panel shows a step, "Looking at the project",
            with a spinner while it runs, a tick once done, or a cross and why
            if it failed, and beneath it the run's output in its
            @{TaskTableScope}. Once found, in its place, the targets found, one
            row each: its icon, its name, and its command, muted, in the
            editor's monospace font, beneath a line saying they were saved to
            .suspense/run.json and that the Code tab has a button for each. A
            failure keeps whatever targets were saved before. "Find again", in
            the header, looks afresh once it is over.

        whileRunning:
            Running a target, the header gives its icon and name, and how it is
            going: a spinner and "Running", "Exited with 0" in the theme's
            success colour, "Exited with N" in its error colour, or "Stopped".
            Beneath it, its command, muted, in the monospace font, and then
            what it prints, its output and its errors together, in the order
            they come, a line each, in the monospace font on the theme's well
            surface, errors not told apart. It scrolls with a
            @{ScrollbarScope} whose lock to the bottom starts on, following the
            latest output. A "Stop" button in the header stops it, and every
            process it started with it, while it runs; once it is over, a
            "Run again" button runs it afresh in its place.

        oneAtATime:
            One target runs at a time. Pressing the button of the target
            running brings back its panel. Pressing another's stops the one
            running and runs the other in its place. Finding the targets while
            one runs stops it.

        minimizing:
            Its minimize button's tooltip says the target keeps running, or
            that the search keeps going. While it runs, it is listed among the
            @{RunningActivityScope}, as "Running" then the target's name, or
            "Finding how to run". Closing the panel stops whatever it holds.

        switchingProjects:
            The panel belongs to the screen rather than its project, so
            switching to another project, as the @{OpenProjectsScope} says,
            stops what it holds and closes it, minimized or not. Quitting
            doesn't ask, and stops it.

    ribbon:
        In the ribbon's Code tab, a "Run" group. Until the project has targets,
        it holds a single full button, "Find How to Run", with a search icon,
        whose tooltip says the harness will look through the project to find
        how it is built, run, and tested. Once it has targets, the group holds
        a button for each, in the order saved, with its kind's icon and its
        name, whose tooltip gives its command: the first a full button, and
        primary, the rest slim. The button of the target running shows a
        spinner in place of its icon. Last, a slim "Find Again" button, with a
        refresh icon, looks afresh. Without a project, as the
        @{NoProjectStateScope} says, the group holds only Find How to Run,
        disabled, its tooltip saying to open a project to run it.

        "Run" as `cargo run`, "Build" as `cargo build`, and "Test" as
        `cargo test`; for a C++ project built with CMake, "Run" as configuring
        and building with `cmake`, then running the binary it built; and so
        on for whatever the project is.

    kinds:
        Each target is of a kind, which picks its icon:
        - run, which runs the project, with a play icon
        - build, which only builds it, with a hammer icon
        - test, which runs its tests, with a flask icon
        - other, anything else, with a terminal icon

    finding:
        overview:
            Nothing about a project's targets is guessed by the application
            itself. Finding them is agentic: a @{OneOffAgentRunScope}, whose
            prompt is run-targets.pi, of the @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}, looks
            through the project, its build files, manifests, and readme, and
            replies with its targets, the way to run the project first. Its
            command runs the project from scratch, building first when it has
            to, so it works on a fresh clone.

        saving:
            Once found, the targets are saved with the project's data, as the
            @{ProjectDataScope} says, in run.json, and read from there from then
            on, every time the project is opened: they aren't found again
            unless asked. run.json is kept with the project, so everyone
            working on it has the same buttons, and can be edited by hand; one
            that can't be read counts as no targets found.

        reply:
            The harness replies with JSON listing each target's name, command,
            and kind. A target with no name or no command is left out, as is a
            kind that isn't one of the four, which counts as other. A reply
            with no targets at all fails, saving nothing.

    panel:
        overview:
            Finding and running are shown in one @{MinimizablePanelScope},
            titled "Run", which holds one thing at a time: finding the targets,
            or running one of them.

        whileFinding:
            While finding, the panel shows a step, "Looking at the project",
            with a spinner while it runs, a tick once done, or a cross and why
            if it failed, and beneath it the run's output in its
            @{TaskTableScope}. Once found, in its place, the targets found, one
            row each: its icon, its name, and its command, muted, in the
            editor's monospace font, beneath a line saying they were saved to
            .suspense/run.json and that the Code tab has a button for each. A
            failure keeps whatever targets were saved before. "Find again", in
            the header, looks afresh once it is over.

        whileRunning:
            Running a target, the header gives its icon and name, and how it is
            going: a spinner and "Running", "Exited with 0" in the theme's
            success colour, "Exited with N" in its error colour, or "Stopped".
            Beneath it, its command, muted, in the monospace font, and then
            what it prints, its output and its errors together, in the order
            they come, a line each, in the monospace font on the theme's well
            surface, errors not told apart. It scrolls with a
            @{ScrollbarScope} whose lock to the bottom starts on, following the
            latest output. A "Stop" button in the header stops it, and every
            process it started with it, while it runs; once it is over, a
            "Run again" button runs it afresh in its place.

            One target runs at a time. Pressing the button of the target
            running brings back its panel. Pressing another's stops the one
            running and runs the other in its place. Finding the targets while
            one runs stops it.

content.text:
Projects can now be run from the ribbon's Code tab. The first time, the harness works out how the project is built, run and tested. That's saved to the project, and from then on each way of running it is a button under Code. `piton check`, `piton format --check` and `piton build` are clean, and 268 of 269 tests pass. The one failure is the same `...`/`…` default-prompt test as before. I haven't tried this in the running app with a real harness run, so the discovery prompt is untested against Claude.

**How it works**
- **Finding (agentic):** until a project has targets, the Code tab has one button, **Find How to Run**. It starts a read-only harness run (the same kind Rescope uses) with a new built-in prompt, `system-prompts/run-targets.pi`.
  - The harness reads the build files, manifests, scripts and readme, and replies with up to eight targets, each a name, a shell command and a kind (run, build, test, other).
  - The first target is how to run the project from a fresh clone. For CMake, that's configure, build, then run the binary.
- **Saved to the project:** the targets go in `.suspense/run.json`. That file is kept with the project, not machine-only, so everyone gets the same buttons, and it can be edited by hand. They're read from there every time the project opens, and only found again if you press **Find Again**.
- **Buttons under Code:** a "Run" group with one button per target, with an icon for its kind. The first target is a large button and stays in the collapsed ribbon. The others are slim, followed by Find Again. Each button's tooltip shows its command, and it shows a spinner while running.
- **Running:** each command runs through `sh -c` in the project folder (`cmd /C` on Windows).
  - Output and errors appear together, line by line, in a minimizable **Run** panel, locked to the bottom.
  - The header shows Running, Exited with N, or Stopped, with **Stop** and **Run again** buttons.
  - Stop kills the whole process group, so child processes stop too.
- **One at a time:** pressing the running target's button only brings its panel back. Pressing a different target stops the running one and starts the new one. It shows in the running-activity list as "Running <name>" or "Finding how to run".

**Choices I made that you may want to change**
- The Run panel belongs to the screen, like Rescope. Switching projects or closing the panel stops the process, and quitting doesn't ask first.
- Discovery is told not to run anything, only read files, so the commands it proposes aren't checked until you press them.
- Nothing asks for confirmation before running a proposed command.

**Spec**
- New scope: `spec/scope/run-targets/index.pi`.
- Updated to point to it: the Code tab, project data (`run.json`), the built-in prompts list, running activity, and the main window.

**Code**
- New: `src/run_targets.rs` (model, saving, parsing the reply, running processes) and `src/run_view.rs` (the panel).
- Changed: `src/ribbon/code_tab.rs` (the tab's commands now depend on the project), `src/ribbon/mod.rs`, `src/main_window.rs`, `src/activity.rs`.

**Tests:** new tests cover:
- reading and saving targets;
- streaming output and stopping a process group;
- finding and saving through the panel, and a run's exit code;
- end to end through the main window: Find How to Run turns into target buttons, and pressing one runs it.

Two existing ribbon tests assumed the Code tab was empty, so I pointed them at the Research tab, which still is.
